metadata.title: Movement Categories
metadata.purpose: Defines the movement skeleton that every TRAIN session is built on. Claude uses this to balance session structure, select exercises from the exercise libraries, and ensure no muscle group or pattern is over or under-trained.

instructions_for_claude.step_1: Identify client goal from client_program_goals.json and map to recommended category balance below
instructions_for_claude.step_2: Select session structure (how many exercises, what categories) based on session_length from onboarding
instructions_for_claude.step_3: Fill each category slot with exercises from the appropriate exercise library
instructions_for_claude.step_4: Check movement_type tags in each exercise (Compound / Isolation / Unilateral) to ensure correct session balance
instructions_for_claude.step_5: Apply equipment filter — only select exercises the client can perform with their available equipment
instructions_for_claude.step_6: Apply mobility and injury filters from client_assessment_schema.json before finalizing
instructions_for_claude.step_7: Use session_position (Primary / Accessory / Finisher) to order exercises correctly within each session

movement_categories.name: Compound Push
movement_categories.definition: Multi-joint pressing movements where force is directed away from the body. Recruits chest, shoulders, and triceps simultaneously.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Every upper body push session. First or second exercise.

goal_priority.fat_loss: Medium — include 1 per upper session in superset
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — anchor of every push day
goal_priority.general_health: Medium — include 1 per session, moderate load

movement_categories.coaching_notes: The foundation of upper body pushing strength. Always cue scapular retraction before any pressing movement. Never program two heavy horizontal pressing movements in the same session without a deload.

movement_categories.name: Compound Pull
movement_categories.definition: Multi-joint pulling movements where force is directed toward the body. Recruits back, biceps, and rear delts simultaneously.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Every upper body pull session. Balance volume with push movements 1:1 or slightly higher pull.

goal_priority.fat_loss: Medium — include 1 per upper session in superset with push
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — back width and thickness anchor
goal_priority.performance: High — critical for athletic force transfer
goal_priority.general_health: High — most people are pull-deficient. Prioritize.

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Most clients are push-dominant and pull-deficient from daily posture. Always match or exceed push volume with pull volume. Vertical pulls (pull-ups, pulldowns) develop lat width. Horizontal pulls (rows) develop thickness and posture.

movement_categories.name: Hip Hinge
movement_categories.definition: Movements initiated by pushing the hips back while maintaining a neutral spine. The most important posterior chain pattern in programming.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Every lower body session. The most undertrained pattern for most clients.

goal_priority.fat_loss: High — massive caloric demand from posterior chain
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — glute and hamstring mass builder
goal_priority.general_health: High — essential for back health and daily movement

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Hip hinge is the pattern most clients have never been properly taught. Spend time here. Key cue: 'Push the floor away with your hips, not your back.' Deadlifts and RDLs are different movements — deadlift from the floor, RDL from the hip. Hip thrust is the king of glute isolation within a hinge pattern.

mobility_flags.hamstring_tightness: Limit range on RDL. Soft knee. Build range over time.
mobility_flags.lower_back_issues: Begin with hip thrust and glute bridge only. Progress to RDL before deadlift.

movement_categories.name: Quad Dominant (Squat Pattern)
movement_categories.definition: Knee-dominant movements where the quads drive force into the ground. Balances the posterior chain emphasis of the hip hinge.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Every lower body session. Pair with hip hinge for complete lower body stimulus.

goal_priority.fat_loss: High — squat pattern burns significant calories and preserves muscle
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — quad and glute mass builder
goal_priority.performance: Critical — foundation of lower body power
goal_priority.general_health: High — functional movement for daily life

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Squat pattern requires more mobility than hinge. Check ankle and hip mobility before loading. Goblet squat is the universal starting point for beginners — it self-corrects posture. Bulgarian split squat is the single best unilateral quad exercise when ready.

mobility_flags.tight_hips: Goblet squat with heel elevation. Widen stance.
mobility_flags.ankle_restriction: Heel elevation (plates under heels or heel-elevated variation). Build ankle mobility.
mobility_flags.knee_issues: Reduce depth. Box squat to control range. Leg press as substitute.

movement_categories.name: Unilateral Lower Body
movement_categories.definition: Single-leg movements that address left/right imbalances, improve stability, and increase core demand. Never skip — most clients have significant asymmetries.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Every lower body session. At least 1 unilateral movement per session.

goal_priority.fat_loss: High — high caloric demand, core engagement

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Always note if client flags left/right imbalance in onboarding. Program unilateral work with weaker side going first. Never let the stronger side compensate for the weaker — match reps exactly. Single-leg RDL is the most functional exercise most clients never do.

mobility_flags.knee_issues: Avoid forward knee travel. Step further forward in lunge. Hip-dominant cuing.
mobility_flags.balance_issues: Use TRX or wall for support initially. Build balance progressively.

movement_categories.name: Unilateral Upper Body
movement_categories.definition: Single-arm pressing or pulling movements. Address shoulder imbalances, increase core anti-rotation demand, and expose weaknesses hidden by bilateral movements.
movement_categories.when_to_program: Include at least once per week per upper body session. Essential for clients with shoulder asymmetry.

goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — eliminates dominant side compensation in upper body
goal_priority.performance: High — sport demands unilateral upper body strength

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Most clients have a dominant arm that takes over in bilateral pressing and rowing. Single-arm work exposes this immediately. Always start with the weaker arm. Note: single-arm dumbbell row is one of the highest-value exercises for back development.

movement_categories.name: Isolation — Upper Body
movement_categories.definition: Single-joint movements targeting a specific muscle with minimal secondary recruitment. Used to address weak links, add volume, and create detail in the muscle.
movement_categories.when_to_program: After compound movements. Never before — isolation pre-fatigue wastes compound movement potential.

goal_priority.fat_loss: Low — prioritize compound. Include 1-2 max per session.
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — 2-4 isolation exercises per session for detail and volume
goal_priority.performance: Low — only when addressing specific weak link
goal_priority.general_health: Low to Medium — include for shoulder health (rear delt, rotator cuff)

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Isolation exercises are finishing work — they add volume and detail, they don't build the foundation. The exception: rear delt and rotator cuff isolation work is essential for shoulder health in almost every client. Lateral raises and rear delt flies should appear in nearly every upper body session regardless of goal.
movement_categories.common_pairing: Paired with opposite isolation in superset (biceps + triceps, chest fly + rear delt)

movement_categories.name: Isolation — Lower Body
movement_categories.definition: Single-joint lower body movements targeting specific muscles. Used to address weak links, add glute/hamstring/quad detail, and round out lower body sessions.
movement_categories.when_to_program: After compound lower body movements. Essential glute isolation for fat loss and muscle gain clients.

goal_priority.fat_loss: Medium — glute isolation finishers add volume without heavy loading
goal_priority.muscle_gain: High — isolation needed to maximize glute and hamstring detail
goal_priority.performance: Low to Medium — hip abduction work for injury prevention
goal_priority.general_health: Medium — hip abductor and adductor work for joint health

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Glute isolation work (kickbacks, abductions) is consistently underestimated. For most female clients, glute isolation finishers are essential — the compound movements alone don't provide enough targeted glute stimulus. Leg curl is the most important and most skipped hamstring isolation exercise.
movement_categories.common_pairing: Glute isolation pairs well with core work in superset

movement_categories.name: Core — Anti-Extension
movement_categories.definition: Core movements that resist the spine being pulled into extension. The most functional core pattern — protects the low back in all pressing, hinging, and carrying movements.
movement_categories.when_to_program: 2-3x per week. Essential for beginners learning to brace. Ab wheel rollout is one of the most effective core exercises available.

goal_priority.fat_loss: High — core engagement in all movements
goal_priority.muscle_gain: Medium — foundational for all heavy compound lifts
goal_priority.performance: Critical — all force transfer goes through the core

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Anti-extension work is more functional than crunches or sit-ups. Teach clients to brace (360-degree pressure, like bracing for a punch) before loading any compound movement. This pattern directly protects the low back.
movement_categories.postpartum_flag: Avoid until diastasis recti is assessed and cleared. Start with dead bug only.

movement_categories.name: Core — Anti-Rotation
movement_categories.definition: Core movements that resist rotational forces. Trains the obliques and deep stabilizers. Essential for athletic performance and spinal health.
movement_categories.when_to_program: 1-2x per week. Often overlooked — essential for athletic populations and anyone with low back history.

goal_priority.muscle_gain: Medium — oblique and deep core development
goal_priority.performance: Critical — rotational force is foundational to all sport
goal_priority.general_health: High — spinal health and posture correction

movement_categories.coaching_notes: The Pallof press is the most underrated core exercise in existence. Simple, safe, and directly trains the anti-rotation pattern that protects the spine under load. Include for any client with low back history.
movement_categories.common_pairing: Pairs well with unilateral lower body

movement_categories.name: Core — Anti-Lateral Flexion
movement_categories.definition: Core movements that resist side-bending forces. Develops the lateral stabilizers — essential for hip stability and reducing low back asymmetries.
movement_categories.when_to_program: 1-2x per week. Often appears in warm-up for hip activation.

goal_priority.performance: High — lateral stability is critical for sport
goal_priority.general_health: Medium — hip and low back health

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Lateral band walks and side planks are some of the best glute medius exercises available. Weak glute medius is a root cause of knee cave in squats and lunges — address early with beginners.

movement_categories.name: Carry & Loaded Movement
movement_categories.definition: Moving with load — the most functional strength pattern. Farmer carries, suitcase carries, overhead carries. Develops grip, core, posture, and full-body stability simultaneously.
movement_categories.when_to_program: 1-2x per week as finisher. Excellent metabolic conditioning tool.

goal_priority.general_health: High — most functional exercise pattern for daily life

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Carries are criminally underused. A heavy 30-second farmer carry at the end of a session is one of the best finishers available — full body, grip, core, posture, and metabolic demand all in one. Start light and focus on posture — tall spine, shoulders back, controlled breath.

movement_categories.name: Explosive & Power
movement_categories.definition: High-velocity movements developing power, rate of force development, and neuromuscular efficiency. Not appropriate for beginners until movement foundations are solid.
movement_categories.session_position: Primary (before strength work) or Conditioning Finisher
movement_categories.when_to_program: Performance and athletic clients primarily. Include for intermediate+ general clients who are cleared and mobile.
movement_categories.experience_requirement: Intermediate to Advanced. Do not program for beginners or clients with joint issues.

goal_priority.muscle_gain: Low — not primary stimulus for hypertrophy
goal_priority.general_health: Low — include only when client is fully cleared and mobile

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Power before strength — always. If including explosive work in a session, it goes first when the CNS is fresh. Never program explosive work when a client is fatigued from heavy compound work.

movement_categories.name: Mobility & Flexibility
movement_categories.definition: Deliberate range of motion work — dynamic in warm-up, static in cooldown. Not optional — integrated into every session.
movement_patterns: Dynamic warm-up (leg swings, hip circles, arm circles, world's greatest stretch)

goal_priority.fat_loss: Medium — keep warm-up brief, prioritize session time
goal_priority.muscle_gain: Medium — joint prep for heavy loading
goal_priority.performance: High — full range of motion required for athletic output
goal_priority.general_health: High — often the primary limiting factor for this population

movement_categories.coaching_notes: Dynamic mobility in warm-up, static stretching in cooldown only. Static stretching before training temporarily reduces force output. The world's greatest stretch is the single most efficient warm-up movement — covers hip flexor, thoracic rotation, ankle, and hamstring in one flow.
movement_categories.mobility_driven_programming: For clients with flagged mobility limitations in onboarding, add 5-10 minutes of targeted mobility to warm-up and program corrective work as accessory movements.

session_structure_templates.description: How to combine categories into a complete session based on split type and session length. Claude uses these as building blocks.

session_order: Explosive or Power (if applicable — performance clients only)
Compound Push OR Compound Pull (alternate each session)
Hip Hinge OR Quad Dominant (alternate each session)
Unilateral Upper Body OR Isolation Upper Body

exercise_count_by_time.30_min: 4-5 exercises — skip finisher and accessory isolation
exercise_count_by_time.75_plus_min: 8-10 exercises — full template with extra isolation or carry

upper_day_order: Mobility & Flexibility (warm-up — shoulder and thoracic focus)
lower_day_order: Mobility & Flexibility (warm-up — hip, ankle, hamstring focus)

goal_category_priority_matrix.description: Quick reference for Claude — which movement categories get the most volume per goal
